title: Getting to Orbit
objective: After this level you can explain that an orbit is falling around a planet, and what escape velocity means.
summary: Orbiting means falling while moving sideways so fast you keep missing. The ISS does it at 28,000 km/h; escaping takes 11.2 km/s.

cards.headline: Astronauts aren’t floating. They’re falling, and missing.
cards.body: Gravity hasn't let go of the space station. It's falling the whole time. It just never hits the ground.

cards.headline: Falling around Earth
cards.body: Throw a ball and Earth's gravity curves it down to the ground. Throw it harder and it lands farther away. Throw it fast enough sideways and the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it falls. That's an orbit: falling forever, and always missing. The International Space Station does this at about 28,000 km/h, circling Earth about every 90 minutes. Around the world in the length of a movie.

cards.headline: Why astronauts float
cards.body: Here's the twist: gravity hasn't switched off up there. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are falling together, so nothing presses them against the floor. You've felt a flicker of this on a roller coaster's first big drop, when your stomach lifts off your seat. Astronauts get that feeling all day, every day.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: gravity hasn't switched off up there. Astronauts float because they're falling.

cards.fact: To leave Earth for good, you need about 11.2 km per second.
cards.context: That's escape velocity: about 40,000 km/h. Anything slower stays with Earth, either falling back or circling like the station. Orbiting means falling and missing. Escaping means leaving for good.

cards.headline: Orbits: understood
learned: An orbit is falling while moving sideways
The ISS circles Earth about every 90 minutes
Astronauts float because they fall together

questions.prompt: Why do astronauts float inside the space station?

options.label: There is no gravity at that height
options.rationale: Gravity in orbit is still strong.

options.label: The station spins to cancel gravity
options.rationale: The station doesn’t spin for gravity.

options.label: They and the station are falling around Earth together
Space is a vacuum, so nothing weighs anything

questions.explanation: Astronauts and their spacecraft fall together around Earth, so nothing pushes them against the floor.

questions.prompt: A probe launches at more than 11.2 km per second. What can it do that the space station can’t?

options.label: Stay in the same spot above Earth
options.rationale: Escaping carries it away, not in place.

options.label: Orbit much closer to the ground
options.rationale: Escape speed takes it away from Earth.

options.label: Float without any gravity acting on it
options.rationale: Gravity still acts on it as it leaves.

options.label: Leave Earth for good instead of orbiting

questions.explanation: At about 11.2 km/s, escape velocity, a spacecraft can break free of Earth’s gravity instead of falling around it.

questions.prompt: From Level 27: which force makes a spacecraft fall around Earth in orbit?

options.label: The Sun’s light pressure
options.rationale: That’s a tiny push, not what shapes an orbit.

options.label: The Moon’s tidal pull
options.rationale: The Moon’s pull is small near Earth.

questions.explanation: Newton’s gravity is what makes an orbiting spacecraft keep falling toward Earth, just like the Moon.
